A novel deep unsupervised learning method, applied to a parameter optimization problem in wireless communications, is presented as an alternative to genetic algorithms. The study focuses on designing the structure of a two-stage relay channel using a two-layer MLP, where the top layer decodes and stores an information symbol and the bottom layer processes the signal. The unsupervised learning approach surpassed genetic algorithms in most scenarios, requiring less than 10% additional training epochs and significantly lower complexity and training time.

We have developed a comprehensive framework to assess the relative importance of individual configurations in the process of beta decay. By comparing the overall beta decay process between two nuclei with differing numbers of neutrons, we can analyze the overall beta decay strength, the distribution of this strength across different energy levels, and the relative impact of collective and particle-like configurations on the beta decay process. This approach has been successfully applied to a range of iron and calcium isotopes to gain a deeper understanding of how these factors evolve across different nuclear configurations.

We examine a model comprising the minimal supersymmetric standard model extended by two Higgs doublets, two additional gauge singlet scalars, and three right-handed neutrinos, with the scalar and neutrino sectors being CPT symmetric. We've analyzed the conditions necessary for the existence of R-parity odd non-relativistic dark matter, whose relic density is determined by singlet scalar contributions, and can also connect with the right-handed neutrinos. Additionally, we've explored a scenario where the dark matter, consisting of R-parity odd particles, can be CPT odd, while one of the fermion singlets acquiring a Majorana mass, and the scalar sector featuring inverse mixing between dark matter and the standard model sector, while its interaction with right-handed neutrinos is mediated through a 'portal' via a scalar.

This paper proposes an algorithm that learns to control complex systems even with limited data available. The method combines the efficiency of inverse dynamics learning and traditional reinforcement learning but leverages inverse dynamics to require fewer training samples. The algorithm's effectiveness is demonstrated through an example of balancing a high-linkage mechanical system, resulting in a $50,000 reduction in research and development costs by reducing the need for physical trials.

We derive the higher-spin symmetry of the Toda conformal field theories by establishing a novel worldsheet path integral framework that inherently preserves higher-spin Ward identities. The theory's higher-spin Ward identities are constructed through a representation of free higher-spin fields on the worldsheet. This approach enables the interpretation of the higher-spin algebra's generators in terms of modes of these fields. Additionally, the worldsheet path integral framework is interpreted as a string theory description of free higher-spin matter fields propagating on a flat background with a large AdS$_2$ component in flat space. These findings are directly related to the string theory duals of CFT$_2$s described by the Toda theory.

To rectify the limitations of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) in generating realistic images, we introduce the Relation Network (R) as a relational component that facilitates communication between adversarial components. With a message-passing mechanism inspired by neural relational architectures, R acts as a connecting medium for GANs. We have successfully integrated R into three types of GANs: a basic GAN using a multilayer perceptron and VAE, and two convolutional GANs with either local or global convolutions. Our experimental results demonstrate that the integration of R enhances the performance of MNDB and MNIST image datasets in comparison to their respective GAN architectures. Furthermore, our analysis of R's message-passing mechanism reveals its key parameters and provides insights for future improvements.

To resolve issues within twin-field quantum key distribution, a novel approach is introduced that overcomes inherent ambiguities in determining light phase by taking advantage of phase symmetry. This approach's effectiveness is demonstrated by modeling the phase and intensity fluctuations of light using complex functions and defining a transformation operator to calculate changes in phase and intensity. This method's accuracy is confirmed by comparing its results to those from twin-field phase reference tests and shows comparable performance.

This work investigates connections between Toeplitz operators within the $p$-Bergman and $p$-Fock spaces and establishes relevant limit operators that act as compressions of Toeplitz operators on specific reproducing Hilbert spaces, namely, the modified Bergman and Fock spaces, modified to be invariant under affine transformations.

This study presents an efficient and effective deep learning approach for
identifying objects within images. Unlike traditional object detection methods
that focus on the overall image, this new technique utilizes simplified object
location markers, known as pseudo bounding-box annotations. By refining these
markers, the proposed method enhances detection accuracy. By training a simple
object detection model using these enhanced annotations, the need for more
time-consuming object detection training is eliminated. Furthermore, the
technique can significantly improve the performance of existing object detection
models. The proposed object proposal technique and the resulting enhanced
detectors achieve impressive results on the PASCAL-VOC dataset, with the
enhanced detectors attaining results on par with state-of-the-art object
proposal and deep learning-based object detection methods.

The extensive $^{12}$CO, $^{13}$CO, and C$^{18}$O line maps across the entire Galactic plane were obtained using the AMI survey. These maps are presented along with the survey's impact on the AMI data, including the influence of self-gravitating gas and the absorption of nearby starlight. To further analyze the data, a novel 'deuterium correction' was introduced to account for line distortions caused by interactions between molecular clouds and neutral hydrogen. Consequently, the observed C$^{18}$O line intensity was multiplied by the average hydrogen-toC$^{18$O ratio. As the motion of gas in the interstellar medium is largely independent of its velocity, this 'hydrogen correction' was performed line-by-line. C$^{18}$O line intensity observations were then compared with $^{12}$CO line intensity, and it was discovered that regions of high hydrogen density, such as those near hot O and B stars, often exhibit significant self-gravitating gas. As the C$^{18}$O line intensity was adjusted, it was observed that the sensitivity of the observations to variations in gas density was significantly improved. Moreover, it was discovered that C$^{18}$O line intensity was correlated with ionized gas density in the high-density regions, and it was calculated that the C$^{18}$O line intensity was approximately 3.0-3.5

Convolutional networks are highly effective in processing visual data, but their benefits are largely due to specific inherent limitations. In this paper, we introduce Transformer models that can be integrated into convolutional networks, replacing the convolutional layers. These transformers are unbiased towards translation, interactive, and capable of handling arbitrary window sizes. By removing convolutional biases, our methods learn inductive structures similar to those found in natural data. It is demonstrated that these transformers can be used to enhance existing models and provide a fully transformer-based alternative. Additionally, our research suggests that transformers have the ability to learn representations that mirror the 2D structure of input data, which is also a key characteristic of convolutions.

This study develops a straightforward method for forecasting mortality rates, building upon classical models incorporating earlier work on factor analysis. By accounting for changing factor correlations over time, the proposed approach outperforms established models, particularly when forecasting mortality rates in longer time periods. Factor analysis is employed to identify hidden drivers influencing mortality rates, which the research finds to be largely similar across different regions and time periods, albeit with varying significance.

In the context of multilingual pre-training, we've discovered that interference during population-based neural architecture search can be a significant issue. To mitigate this interference, we've developed two methods: population size optimization and interference-free model merging. Our proposed methods achieved impressive performance improvements of 10.1% and 7.1%, respectively, compared to the baseline version of RoBERTa and ELECTRA that underwent neural architecture search.

A significant number of machine learning feature extraction methods rely on time-series feature extraction techniques.  However, current popular open-source libraries for time-series feature extraction are plagued by several issues.  They demand a high level of coding proficiency due to their command-line interface, consume excessive memory, and require extensive coding knowledge.  Furthermore, many lack the ability to efficiently handle large datasets through parallel processing techniques such as multiprocessing or distributed computing.  To resolve these problems, we have developed the `theft` Python package, offering both command-line and object-oriented interfaces for a range of time-series feature extraction techniques, including `tsfs`, `tsfresh`, and our own contributions.  Key features of `theft` include the ability to run extraction processes across multiple CPU cores, the generation of HTML reports, the option to cluster and perform hypothesis testing on datasets, and the ability to save and load intermediate results to streamline processing.

We prove that geodesic completeness in a CAT(0) space's geometric action corresponds to its fundamental group being of finite rank and meeting certain other criteria. This result then leads to the conclusion that geodesic completeness holds for a lattice within a simple CAT(0) group. As a consequence, the closed quotient of this lattice by the rest of the lattice inherits geodesic completeness. We specifically show that closed quotients of Chevalley-Steinberg lattices over local fields, when finitely many Iwasawa components are included, are geodesically complete.

This paper details our approach for translating quality assessment at machine translation shared task 1. We analyze the performance metrics of three models: consensus model, herd model, and human judge, evaluating their effectiveness across three dimensions: consistency, correlation with human assessment, and efficiency.

The paper describes the methodologies employed in ensuring the reliability of various models' assessments. Furthermore, our findings reveal that the consensus model exhibits the highest correlation with human evaluation scores in both single and multiple sentence contexts, but the herd model excels in terms of efficiency due to its ability to process translations quickly without sacrificing much in terms of correlation. Lastly, we propose a combination of assessment metrics from the consensus and herd models that can effectively accelerate translation quality assessment while maintaining high accuracy and human relevance.

Intense and uniform wave patterns seen in certain systems like lasers can be explained using a coherent superposition of zero-intensity eigenmodes. These intense wave patterns are crucial applications in technologies like lithography and optical trapping. However, designing systems that generate these wave patterns has been a complex task, even more so when dealing with systems like lasers where wave patterns and system parameters influence each other reciprocally. To address this issue, we developed an effective design method for a coherent light source, or collimated light emitter, that generates these uniform wave patterns in a parallel plate system. By optimizing the light source design, we were able to achieve wave patterns with a high level of uniformity, as demonstrated in numerical simulations.

Neural networks are often complex and consume significant resources, but there's a growing need to make them more efficient, especially in visual tasks. Research has shown that reducing the importance of certain weights in a network can significantly improve its performance without compromising accuracy. We've extended this idea to achieve high-precision results in visual recognition tasks. By applying an iterative method to remove certain weight components, we're able to create much smaller versions of large neural networks that perform nearly as well as the original. Notably, we've found that large versions of ResNet-50 and ViT-B/16 can be reduced to just 15% of their original weight without losing more than 0.5% in their accuracy on image classification tasks, with similar results seen in other visual tasks like object detection and semantic segmentation. Furthermore, we've discovered that large versions of neural networks with mixed integer precision consume only 15% more than small versions, significantly less than the over 50% difference typically observed. These findings indicate that removing the weights of large neural networks can be a viable strategy for creating more efficient and effective visual models.

This study examines European lotteries from a consumer's perspective to identify which tickets yield positive returns. By combining a mathematical model of lottery ticket returns with data on European lotteries, we found that tickets drawn in the later stages of each lottery have positive returns during approximately 17.5% of draws, with high-value tickets (€10 and above) returning positive values in only around 5% of cases. Simulations suggest that an optimal strategy of reusing previously drawn tickets can return €11 on average for each dollar spent, outperforming both lotteries and online gambling.

The four-parameter generalized O(N) model is used to derive the critical behavior of its non-symmetric phase using a large-charge expansion in the specific heat. This results in large-charge expansions for the critical temperature and correlation length, as well as the critical exponents delta, nu, and eta. These findings are in agreement with those from Monte-Carlo simulations, with calculated critical exponents differing by less than 10% and showing a trend that could lead to further discrepancy reduction. The heat capacity analysis also indicates a second-order phase transition, with derived critical exponents differing from the symmetric phase. This study also provides a large-charge expansion for the inverse magnetic susceptibility, which shows a non-universal behavior and could be used to determine magnetic ordering.

In non-zero strain environments, transport in the valley Hall effect is influenced by mechanical deformation which may vary across space. Existing research has primarily focused on rigid valley Hall effects, ignoring the impact of strain environment variability. Our work examines how changes in the valley Hall distribution function and current vary when environmental deformations and sample geometry changes are taken into account. By considering these factors, we identify conditions under which their influence becomes significant. Our analysis also includes a comparison between geometric variations and environmental deformations on valley currents in both constant and localized cases, and we discuss how one can manipulate the valley currents by adjusting environmental deformations.

The limited availability of annotated data in computer vision hampers researchers, making it crucial to develop methods for addressing this challenge. Although domain adaptation methods have been developed to tackle this issue, they often struggle with generalization, as they become overly specialized for target domains. A potential solution is to create domain adaptive models with better generalization capabilities. Drawing inspiration from ensemble methods, researchers proposed the "model soup" scheme, which combines multiple models' weights to achieve both higher interpretability and generalization. In this study, we apply the model soup method to address a crucial problem in computer vision, namely domain adaptation, and achieve state-of-the-art results on multiple datasets, including CIFAR-Labeled, CIFAR-Unlabeled, CIFAR-All, STL10-Unlabeled, and STL0-All. Furthermore, we develop a novel method, SOA, that achieves superior performance on CIFAR-Labeled and STL10-Labeled datasets, competing with a strong baseline that includes both domain adaptation and domain augmentation methods.

Recent comparisons of embedding algorithms indicate that t-SNE overemphasizes local connections, particularly between closely situated data points on spherical data, leading to poor preservation of global relationships when visualized in three dimensions. We contend that effectively prioritizing nearby points necessitates employing a suitable distance measure across all data points, not just the nearest ones. Consequently, our proposed method involves adapting t-SNE by substituting the Gaussian distribution with a Peircian distribution, which downweights distant data points and upweights those in proximity. We introduce two distributions, both parameterized with a single non-negative constant and tailored for spherical data, which include the Peircian distribution and a variant with an additional decay term. The initial distribution achieves optimal nearest neighbor preservation when its parameter reaches infinity, while the second distribution further prioriters these neighbors with minimal detriment to data relationships at greater distances. Through numerical evaluations, we ascertain that our revised approaches enhance visualizations by revealing previously obscured relations within image datasets, including the MNIST and CelebA datasets.

We examine the strong-coupling behavior of a polaron in a two-dimensional Fermi sea to several components of the full diagrammatic expansion, yielding a quantitative analysis across various coupling strengths. For the entire series, the polaron $Z$ factor significantly surpasses a weak-coupling approximation based on a single-particle and -hole excitation, the former converging to $Z\sim\alpha^{1/2}$, the latter $Z\sim\alpha^{1/3}$. For the polaron energy, the weak-coupling result shows a marked deviation from more comprehensive, accurate many-body numerical calculations.

The Fermi-Hubbard model is a complex computational problem that's at the core of understanding high-temperature superconductivity. Due to this challenge, numerical simulations are difficult to conduct. Digital-analog quantum computing offers a more feasible option by leveraging a combination of conditional gates and a global Hamiltonian to initiate a complex model's dynamics. This method allows for the efficient simulation of systems with a large number of qubits, which can't be achieved using a completely digital approach. Our study showcases this capability by simulating the Fermi-Hubbard model on a hardware device using digital-analog quantum computing. By controlling a specific global potential on a 4-qubit hardware, we're able to control an effective Hubbard model with tunable parameters. Our results show that using digital-analog quantum computing, we can accurately predict the model's behavior up to a certain time frame, which is an important milestone in quantum algorithm development.

Research has shown that bipartite complete graphs and complete bipartite graphs along with one edge removal have uniquely identifiable matching polynomials, a concept known as a strong automorphism group. This study builds on that work, determining other graphs that share this strong matching property, specifically focusing on full bipartite graphs, full bipartite graphs minus one edge, complete star graphs, and complete bipartite graphs minus two edges; results of the strong matching property for the last two cases rely on a newly formulated system of equations.

The underlying reason why certain quantum representations exhibit asymptotic behavior aligned with pseudo-Anosov elements remains unknown. The use of quantum representations, particularly in the context of surface surgeries, has been instrumental in addressing the strong finiteness problem. However, the connection between the existence of asymptotic behavior in quantum representations and the occurrence of pseudo-Anosov dynamics remains unclear, despite their established roles in related problems.

This study aims to contribute to the existing body of knowledge on information systems research by examining how organizations utilize Scrum in a remote work setting, and whether the adoption of Scrum methodologies can contribute to project success. Conducted through two case studies involving organizations that transitioned to remote work during the COVID-19 pandemic, the research employs a qualitative approach to gather in-depth insights into the experiences of respondents. By gathering and analyzing open-ended responses from IT project managers, the findings reveal that organizations of varying sizes can effectively implement Scrum methodologies for successful project delivery, even when working remotely. Additionally, the study highlights the importance of selecting appropriate tools and fostering open communication to facilitate collaboration and ensure clear understanding among team members.

This paper delves into the computational complexity of the determinant's algebraic degree and the exact degree of its minimal polynomial for the characteristic matrix of an integer arrowback matrix of size $n$, a class of matrices with $n$ identical rows and distinct rows of size $n-1$, whose characteristic matrix has the property of being an integer arrowup matrix. We find that the minimal polynomial of the characteristic matrix of an integer arrowback matrix has the maximum possible degree $n$, with its coefficient set containing at least $\frac{n}{4}$ non-zero elements. Furthermore, our study reveals the Tridiagonal Matrix Lemma's generalization and the derivation of the characteristic polynomial for integer arrowback matrices of size $n$.

The proper decay lengths of beauty and charm particles, along with other relevant data, have been studied. A notable finding revealed that the mean lengths of beauty hadrons exceed those of charm hadrons and other sources by a significant margin. The reported uncertainties in the measurements of beauty proper decay lengths were observed to be lower than the differences between theoretical predictions and experimental results. The data presented in this study were compiled by the \mbox{AMBER} collaboration and can be accessed through \mbox{AMBER}'s \mbox{HEPLUG} system.

This paper introduces an advanced method of topological data analysis called topological color-based machine learning, which allows for data sets with multiple color labels to be analyzed effectively. Traditional topological data analysis methods rely on a single similarity metric, limiting their application to certain types of data sets. To overcome this limitation, we propose a new approach that utilizes color-based persistent homology to identify connections between distinct color classes, as well as a graph-based method tailored for small data volumes. Our approach is demonstrated through case studies involving artificial examples and real-world applications, specifically analyzing handwritten digit datasets and gene expression data. Through these applications, we show that topological color-based machine learning can enhance existing techniques and even serve as a standalone predictive tool.

This study investigates the binary power control method where base stations decide whether to transmit or remain silent, based on a set of switchable rules. We derive a theoretical approximation for this policy in a complex network with a significant number of base stations and user pairs, by first simplifying the interaction between neighboring cells to a single control variable that represents the power ratio. We then utilize random graph theory to develop a equation that predicts the power control outcome, which is a sum over a simulated network where each base station's decision depends on its own ratio and the ratios of other active base stations, ultimately determining its silence or transmission state. Through analysis and simulation, we demonstrate that this equation accurately reflects the binary policy, and evaluate its performance. Surprisingly, we found that binary power control outmaneuvers optimal power control, achieving similar throughput with less computational requirements. We have also identified specific policies and their applications in reducing interference and optimizing network connectivity.

The vast availability of accounting data has led to the emergence of numerous novel business concepts, including the concept of segmenting accounts into distinct segments based on their underlying purposes. However, detecting these purposes within accounts is a challenging task that necessitates the assignment of a confidence level to these purposes, which can be achieved through the application of advanced mathematical techniques such as the Dempster-Shafer mass. To facilitate this task, we propose a method that leverages the characteristics of the accounts and applies statistical methods to determine the confidence levels associated with each account's purpose. This mass is then used to represent the interest of the assignee in each account's purpose, which can be applied to the development of an efficient and effective auditing process.

A new approach, Acceptance Rejection Stitching, is developed for generating point process realizations within a given area, utilizing local models at specific points. This method combines the local models through acceptance rejection criteria, allowing it to work with any point process having a known density, even if that density is only partially available. Through simulation on the Cox Rebirth process, it's demonstrated that ARS yields more accurate results than alternative methods like simulation concatenation and recursive stitching, particularly when using a limited number of models. Furthermore, an application of this method to realistic data and a case study with two distinct processes reveals that ARS produces outcomes comparable to simulated annealing, a method considered the benchmark in this context.

In the context of Generalized Uncertainty Principle (GUP), deformed Galilean transformations are derived from the requirements of preserving energy and momentum as well as momentum. These transformations exhibit a similarity to Lorentz transformations, with a specific limit where $\hbar G(s) p \gtrsim 1$. Additionally, these new transformations result in deformed Newton-Cartesian structures where geodesic motion, determined by the metric tensor constructed from the Sagnac metric with general coordinates, aligns with the conservation of generalized momentum.

In task scheduling for multitasking systems, task processing needs to be matched with available computing resources. Current scheduling algorithms often assume a constant rate of available computing power, ignoring the dynamic task scheduling process itself. To address this limitation, our research explores a novel resource-aware scheduling approach that considers available computing power as a variable in task scheduling. By modeling the task scheduling process as a Markov Decision Process and incorporating the available computing power ratio into the reward function, we developed a deep reinforcement learning-based policy. This new approach outperforms traditional algorithms like Earliest Deadline First in various scenarios.

This study investigates controlled hopping of a single rigid link supported by a single spring on a soft surface. The control strategy involves regulating the spring's force to accurately follow a pre-established path that同步 with the surface's natural response to the hop. Various methods for anticipating the surface's displacement are considered along with a range of control implementations. The outcomes indicate that feedback control surpasses open-loop control in achieving trajectory synchronization, even when incorporating substantial model inaccuracies. Moreover, real-world implementation errors can be mitigated through feedback control. The investigation also explores the feasibility of utilizing finite element models to generate the optimal hopping trajectory and reveals that such models can effectively generate trajectory plans that perform better than those derived from simplified models that fail to account for the ground's behavior.

In modern IoT settings, over-the-air firmware updates are essential for maintaining successful operations. Current solutions are often limited by their ability to efficiently and reliably update large networks of IoT devices. This paper suggests a novel approach called Concurrent Transmission (CT) for increasing the efficiency and dependability of firmware updates in large-scale IoT deployments. By allowing multiple devices to simultaneously download and process update packets, CT enhances the scalability of the network, reduces the time required for each device to apply the new firmware, and minimizes the risk of transmission errors. A CT-based protocol is designed to enhance the efficiency and reliability of firmware updates over Wi-Fi networks, ensuring that all devices successfully receive and apply the new updates. The effectiveness of CT is evaluated against existing over-the-air update solutions, with the results showing significant improvements in the efficiency, reliability, and performance of the proposed method.

A novel method, rooted in the concept of fractal dimensions, is used to investigate many-body localization transitions in both discrete and continuous space systems. Focusing on the disordered discrete-time quantum walk with a thermal to many-body localization phase transition, our research reveals that the fractal dimension linked to the self-energy varies between 0.536 and 0.626 at the transition threshold, a value obtained independently of system size or impurity density. Moreover, the observed fractal dimension aligns with mean-field predictions, and the investigation also exposes the characteristics of the critical exponent related to the localization length at the transition threshold, which spans from 2.23 to 2.68, a value also determined without relying on the extent of the system or the density of impurities.

A new algorithm, 'kBM-DP+', was developed to solve the MultipleTargets problem, 
  which involves determining the shortest path between two points on a grid 
  that avoids k moving obstacles, in a more efficient manner. Initially, a 
  decision problem variant of this problem was solved using dynamic programming 
  with a time complexity of O(k^2k^(3d+2)) and space complexity of 
  O(k^2kd), in contrast to the previous best approach of k^(5d+1) complexity. 
  However, this was further improved by introducing 'kBM-DP+' with reduced 
  complexity, in a more space and time efficient manner. Moreover, a new 
  'kBM-BFS' algorithm was proposed for decision problems with time complexity 
  of O(k^(2d)) and for the search problem with time complexity of 
  O(k^(2d)k^(d)) and space complexity of O(k^(3d)).

Machine learning models, including those based on quantum algorithms, are highly susceptible to adversarial examples - subtle input alterations that drastically distort predictive accuracy. Despite the growing reliance on AI for decision-making, the underlying causes of this phenomenon remain poorly understood. This research delves into the connection between neural network classifiers and the mentioned adversarial effect. It then assesses the robustness of quantum classifiers - specifically those using quantum support vector machines and quantum marginal maximum likelihood methods - in comparison to their classical counterparts. The study employed image classification benchmarks, such as MNIST and CIFAR-10, and discovered that all classifiers, both quantum and classical, are vulnerable to adversarial examples. Notably, it was found that quantum classifiers' predictions can deviate entirely from reality, often with minimal input distortion.

The research involves examining the asymptotic behavior of volume-normalized Steklov eigenvalues in a family of domains closely related to a sphere as it converges to a lower-dimensional space. Previous studies have provided partial results under various assumptions, and this paper aims to resolve issues arising from integer Steklov eigenvalues. Specifically, this paper demonstrates that in a converging sequence of almost spherical domains, a modified Steklov operator converges to a Dirichlet Laplacian operator on a specific space as a convergence criterion is met.

Process execution analysis relies on alignments between processes and their respective models, but existing methods have specific limitations. Certain alignments require the entire execution to fit within a single model trace, whereas others only need sufficient prefix or suffix models to match certain parts of the execution. New infix and postfix alignments address these issues, focusing on matching central or trailing parts of an execution respectively, allowing for more flexibility. However, this comes with a cost - for infix alignments, two sufficient prefix and suffix model traces are needed, whereas postfix alignments only need one sufficient prefix trace. We'll demonstrate the flexibility of infix and postfix alignments by applying them to process execution analysis and then show how they can improve efficiency in model verification.

This paper introduces the concept of leveraging deep neural networks to enhance the simulation of how radio waves propagate through space. To achieve this, the researchers utilized the widely used Longley-Rice propagation model along with the deeply nested networks (DeepNN) approach to develop a more efficient simulation model. By training the DeepNN model using data from the Longley-Rice model, the researchers were able to replicate non-line-of-sight radio propagation patterns, including those of clustered, radio signal data, resulting in significant improvements in accuracy and reduced computational complexity. When comparing the DeepNN-based model to the traditional model, the results showed reduced computational requirements and increased precision in radio signal simulations.

This study explores the role of validation algorithms in enhancing online temporal planning systems and demonstrates their potential to be leveraged in existing planning systems for improvement. To this end, we examine three temporal planning algorithms, which are designed to verify solutions for a particular encoding of the planning and validation problem. By examining the performance of these algorithms on the STRIPS-Relaxed benchmark, we find that they can be effectively employed to optimize relaxation-based planning heuristics. By incorporating a time-aware goal ordering method and the capability to prune infeasable time points, we are able to create more accurate and efficient heuristics. By integrating these validation-derived heuristics into high-performance planners such as GraphSearch, GraphLandmark, and GSUB, we observe significant performance gains. Additionally, we investigate the use of these validation algorithms to analyze and optimize classical planning models.

This study investigates the impact of allocating generation capacities out of phase with demand peaks using the US Western Interconnection as a model for a highly integrated power system. It employs the Energy Systems Planning Tool to simulate multiple scenarios, prioritizing the simulation of real-world operations. The research demonstrates that simulating the system with higher time-resolution significantly amplifies the negative effects of misallocating generation capacities. Specifically, a system designed with 15-minute intervals reveals more pronounced consequences of misallocations compared to annual models. An annual-model allocation of 80 GW of generation capacity that could avoid future capacity shortages during peak periods actually results in a substantial net loss when simulated with higher time-resolution. Furthermore, different simulation resolutions lead to significantly varying forecasts of needed capacity expansions. When simulating the US Western Interconnection with higher time-resolutions, it demonstrates that needs for generation capacity may decrease substantially.

We analyze one-dimensional Vlasov-Poisson models involving ionic models and apply either zero or non-zero boundary conditions to the Poisson equations. For the ionic models, ion velocities are derived according to specific rules that either ensure particle conservation or not. Under certain conditions related to entropy and given non-equilibrium Maxwellian distributions, our work demonstrates that solutions are stable and converge asymptotically to the global equilibrium through the H-theorem and an entropy method.

This paper outlines our approach to determining relevant search terms from proposed change tasks in controlled natural language (CNCL) format. We propose that our proposed approach, which combines the RANK features R1 and R2 with the POS features, outperforms the current industry standard. The RANK and POS features collectively enable the identification of suitable search terms. To achieve this, we designed and implemented two distinct approaches, AdA and AdB, that operate in two stages: initially, AdA identifies and eliminates stop words based on a customized list, while AdB uses a mechanism that predicts stop words based on a distinct flag. In the second stage, AdA applies the TextRank and POSRank algorithms to rank the remaining terms, with both positive and negative flags considered, while AdB applies a single Pos system flag. We evaluated our approach on 100,000 lines of code from three programming languages, C#, Java, and C++, and our results indicate a 20% increase in the identification of relevant search terms. Our findings suggest that our proposed approach can significantly enhance the search capabilities of software change tasks.

The behavior of ultrasound within rheo-acoustic gels when assisted is not yet fully grasped,
limiting our understanding of how these gels break or change structure in response to ultrasound.
To address this knowledge gap, a numerical approach was employed to simulate the forces exerted by low-intensity ultrasound within various models of these gels.
A standard model of wave propagation was integrated with two different representations of porous materials to investigate the effects of different levels of gas entrapment.
Results showed that the behavior of the forces changes significantly depending on the gas level within the material and the frequency of the ultrasound, deviating from previous assumptions.
Moreover, the regions where the forces are most pronounced in more complex models closely resemble the patterns observed in granular materials under similar ultrasound conditions.
These findings suggest that the way in which ultrasound causes material changes is highly dependent on the specific characteristics of the material and may be influenced by the way in which energy is not uniformly distributed within the material.
The research demonstrates the application of mathematical induction to establish the Collatz conjectration, employing a comprehensive approach that takes into account all possible outcomes.

The growth of digital archives and the subsequent need to categorize documents into relevant topics has made machine learning a crucial tool in document classification. However, machine learning models often operate as "black boxes," making it difficult to grasp their decision-making processes. The rise of Explainable AI has made it possible to delve deeper into these algorithms, thus enhancing our comprehension of their decision-making processes. The following paper explores various explainability methods that contribute to document classification understanding. Furthermore, the need to integrate explainability methods into the machine learning pipeline to fully interpret machine learning models is also explored in this research.

We have developed two novel extensions to the stable matchings model: (i) the Stable Matchings with Ratings model explores how public evaluations affect agent utility in large markets, and (ii) the Matching with Ratings model relaxes the stability concept to account for public ratings. Public evaluations are assumed to be accurate and have no noise. In the former model, we demonstrate that, in large random markets, public evaluations often significantly impact agents' utility. Conversely, in the latter model, public ratings fail to move towards truthful evaluations. Moreover, in both models, truthful evaluations do not necessarily lead to a socially optimal outcome. Finally, we propose a mechanism to incentivize agents to provide accurate ratings.

Automated scoring of summarization outputs is a long-standing issue in NLP that has been addressed by existing metrics like ROUGE, BLEUT,BERTScore and others. These metrics rely on comparing the summaries to reference material or embedding similarities. However, these methods have several drawbacks, such as low diversity and correlation with human scoring. To address these issues, we introduce SummScore, a neural automated scoring model that achieves significant improvements of up to 16% and 12% over state-of-the-art methods in summary diversity and correlation with human scoring, respectively. Additionally, SummScore exhibits correlation gains of up to 26% over existing metrics when evaluated on datasets with high diversity. Furthermore, SummScore's performance is complemented by a set of 1000 evaluation dimensions derived from word association analysis, which we also make available.

To study how signal reconstruction methods work when data is imperfect, we're examining how one type of imaging - computed tomography - can efficiently rebuild complex signals from diverse sources, like the parts of a signal separated by significant differences. We've made two key findings: first, as the amount of data from these distinct parts increases, the amount of signal that can be efficiently rebuilt also grows. Second, we've discovered that an existing signal rebuilding approach called SPARSiS performs better than other methods like compressed sensing in this type of imaging, particularly in rebuilding complex signals with distinct parts. We've also found that SPARSiS performs better than traditional tomographic reconstruction methods, producing clearer images and more accurate images, in addition to being faster and simpler to implement.

This work presents a novel, robust multi-modal fusion approach for object detection during sensor failures in self-driving vehicles. Called BEVfusion, this method combines images and point cloud data in the background to effectively handle modalities failing at different times and locations. Based on the proposed fusion framework, a resilient system achieves +22.4% recall and +11.3% accuracy (absolute) for object detection in the case of camera failures, and +48.6% recall and +26.1% accuracy (absolute) for object detection in the case of LiDAR failures, within the 200m range, using the nuScenes dataset.

We introduce a fluctuating turbulence model, based on the fluctuating hydrodynamics (FH) concept, which integrates passive scalar transport into the fluid dynamics framework. Building on this approach, FH offers a complementary continuous model to FHDS for understanding the dynamics of turbulent flows and scalar fields within fluid systems. Through this study, it is shown that a key property of a widely-used discrete-to-continuous model, the "energy cascade model" (ECM), is already inherent in FH. By accounting for the energy transfer between kinetic and scalar energy, FH effectively captures the cross-spectral coupling that occurs in turbulent flows. Furthermore, in high-Reynolds number regimes, FH is found to converge to the deterministic Navier-Stokes equation in the absence of thermal fluctuations, while simultaneously providing enhanced dissipation capabilities that go beyond the capabilities of the deterministic Navier-Stokes equation. These findings are supported by 2D and 3D numerical simulations of passive scalar transport in turbulent flows.

We've conducted an experiment where a laser interacts with a fluid heated by a separate, higher-powered laser, a phenomenon that occurs when boiling occurs. As the cooling process creates a fluid with varying densities, it causes the test laser to exhibit striking visual effects, including the formation of rings, patterns, and irregular waves. Moreover, a simulation program has been able to recreate these rings, patterns, and irregular waves in response to fluid movements. Interestingly, the simulation closely matches both visual observations and data on the intensity of the test laser.

The analysis of patent archives reveals valuable design patterns, enabling multiple stations in a large organization to maintain consistency in their designs. Nonetheless, current design mining approaches often overlook the complexity and diversity of patent designs, which comprise 1) a broad range of individual projects and their specific design attributes and 2) a fragmented and incomplete representation of individual design steps and outcomes. These limitations can lead to unstable conclusions that do not generalize across different projects. To address these issues, this study introduces a novel design mining framework that emphasizes logical design reasoning and modular design structure analysis to enhance stability and applicability. To demonstrate its effectiveness, we apply this framework to extract design patterns from patent archives related to a specific type of cooling fan, comparing the results to those from a traditional approach and demonstrating significant improvements in stability and relevance to modern design projects.

The proliferation of IoT devices has led to a significant increase in data generation, posing challenges for processing and analyzing these data. To overcome the limitations associated with traditional data processing techniques, such as the difficulty in handling the rapid increase in data volume and speed, these challenges are redefined as minimizing data processing costs and adapting to real-time processing. To this end, we have reimagined data streams as observations of dynamic systems and proposed a novel framework called H-STREAM, which treats these dynamic systems as ergodic and employs statistical methods to efficiently extract insights from the data. By leveraging these methods, H-STREAM can achieve real-time processing with improved data representation, effectively addressing the speed and volume constraints associated with data streams while increasing the cost of processing.

A new type of quark, specifically a vector-like quark, is a hypothetical particle that could potentially be responsible for the existence of beyond the standard model particles. To investigate the feasibility of this new quark, a numerical model called NNAJD was created, which estimates the probability of producing pairs of these new quarks through the exchange of weak bosons at a high-energy environment. To simplify the calculation to just the interactions involving the standard model particles, a specific gauge choice was selected. The estimated probability was then compared against a more comprehensive numerical model and found to be quite accurate, with differences less than 10 percent, even in cases where new quarks have very high masses. To further simplify the calculation, the NNAJD model can be integrated into a more comprehensive model to obtain more precise results.

This research contributes a pre-trained Transformer-based generator that can translate SPARQL queries from natural language sentences. The model utilizes Knowledge Graph (KG) information for entity and relation alignment, aligning it with recent methods for KG reading comprehension. However, distinct from existing approaches, we investigate NLS2SPARQL and incorporate the problem's constraints to prevent the generation of invalid queries. A parser-based technique is used to identify the query's syntax structure, which assists in predicting the query's underlying syntax. Additionally, we integrate a copy mechanism for terms not present in the vocabulary, thereby increasing the model's performance. Experiments on the OpenKG and FLOPS datasets demonstrate the superiority of our method, with the former showing a 26.6% increase in F1-score and the latter a 23.6% rise in hit rate, compared to previous methods.

Our research focuses on the evolution of Computer Science research through a examination of publishing trends. We identify limitations of current methods that rely solely on automatic venue classification and created a new approach that uses human expertise to analyze and understand publishing patterns. We then applied both methodologies to the Internet Structure field to compare their effectiveness. The results indicate that considering venue reputation is crucial for accurately tracking the development of research areas over time. We identified distinct periods of growth and decline, as well as connected subfields within the Internet Structure community.

Ensuring that complex control systems are robust against uncertainties and potential failures is a significant challenge in applications involving human safety, such as autonomous vehicles. Traditional control systems are being replaced by neural networks, but their intricate nature makes it difficult to guarantee safety and reliability. Drawing from the success of verification methods used in computational geometry, symbolic reachability analysis has become a powerful tool in analyzing neural network-based control systems. Meanwhile, computer vision and machine learning communities have seen remarkable advancements in verifying neural network robustness against potential adversarial attacks. This research aims to leverage these advancements to develop a more efficient and thorough verification process for neural network-based control systems, leveraging state-of-the-art adversarial robustness techniques to enhance safety and reliability.

Functorial clustering schemes have been proposed to mitigate certain limitations in traditional clustering methods. Nonetheless, these schemes suffer from distinct shortcomings similar to those associated with greedy clustering. To overcome these, a particular scheme was found to have limitations, particularly concerning inaccuracies in unweighted metric spaces. Our proposed extension of these clustering schemes addresses some of these issues, specifically concerning inaccuracies affecting single-linkage clustering.

The task of reconstructing missing data in a video stream through tensor completion is simplified into smaller, manageable image-based tasks. Current approaches tackle each image separately, but our research demonstrates that splitting the video into frames undermines tensor completion's effectiveness in cases of motion. In response, we leverage the temporal connections within the video to enhance its completion. Specifically, we utilize frame differences to facilitate easier tensor completion and improve the video's overall reconstruction quality, validated by experimental results.

Within rotating fluids, rotating turbulence generates inertial waves leading to a verified $E(k) \propto \epsilon_{\omega}^{2/3}k^{-5/3}\sin^2(k_{\perp}r^{-1})$ power spectrum, first predicted by Goto. Researchers recreated this spectrum through numerical simulations at various Rossby numbers, yielding an additional, previously unobserved low-wavenumber side lobe in the spectrum, which vanishes at high Rossby numbers. The inertial wave spectrum primarily comprises the expected $k_{\perp}$-space component, with a prediction of a potential $e^{-\alpha\mathrm{Ro}^2} \epsilon_{\omega}^{4/3}\sin^4(k_{\perp}\sin(\mathrm{arccos}(-\mathrm{Ro})/2))$ side lobe at low $k$ and high Rossby numbers.

We and others have recently found that many practical optimization problems can be effectively modeled using graph structures. In many graph optimization tasks, a preprocessing step called graph normalization, which iteratively removes redundant nodes and edges, often leads to improved performance. Although the theoretical underpinnings of this process are still poorly understood, in our work we demonstrate that its iterations correspond to finding maximum weight independent sets in certain subgraphs. Additionally, our findings show that its outcomes can be predicted in linear time and provide a theoretical basis for its success in various practical scenarios.

We've performed an exact calculation in the study of electrically modulated graphene subjected to a magnetic field oriented perpendicularly. This combination generates both Landau levels (LL) and oscillating patterns. Our findings reveal that these patterns align with previously established studies. A key aspect of this calculation involves accounting for the discontinuous potential within the system's Hamiltonian. As such, we addressed this issue by applying both the Landau-level and envelope-function approaches. Both methods yielded identical results, confirming the validity of each. Our study demonstrates the utility of these calculations in determining the band structure of various two-dimensional materials, including transition metal dichalcogenides, that can be integrated into electronic devices.

New 7.8 GHz radio observations of the M dwarf binary CR Draconis were conducted using the GMRT in 2019, revealing enhanced emission in both optical and polarized forms compared to earlier findings. Compared to Jupiter, CR Draconis exhibits greater total radio emission but less structured emission. Additionally, the observed polarization characteristics indicate that CR Draconis exhibits polarization levels comparable to or exceeding those of Jupiter.

To effectively learn complex, flexible models from unstructured images, recent research has shown significant promise. However, current approaches are primarily limited to modeling static objects. In our work, we demonstrate how Articulated Neural Rendering can efficiently learn the motion and dynamics of moving objects, including those with flexible parts, by incorporating a method to model non-rigid movement. Additionally, we extend its applicability to scenarios with occlusions, a common occurrence when a single view cannot fully reveal an object's appearance. Our framework also allows for the direct estimation of camera movement and position, a feature particularly beneficial in uncontrolled environments. Our computational model, implemented using backpropagation, produces visually accurate and physically consistent results, surpassing human-level performance.

Human visual systems are capable of identifying objects even when they undergo significant image transformations such as color changes and increased blur. To investigate this phenomenon, we created a new, challenging dataset, known as EXTREME, which features extreme image distortions. We employed a randomized forest-based approach to create new versions of images from the ImageNet database using a combination of strong image manipulation tools, including AlphaBlender, Numpy, and Colorizer. We evaluated various artificial neural network designs and found that NONE-ResNet was the top-performing model. We used EXTREME to train human-based and machine-based visual recognition systems and discovered that humans outperform the NONE-ResNet model, even with the distorted images. We observed a notable difference in the way that humans and machine-based models process data, which could have significant implications for the development of more efficient and effective machine learning models.

It's been observed that specific Wilson loops of the Chern-Simons theory with gauge group $SU(2)$ and complex deformation, when evaluated at quantized values, are exactly equal to the corresponding generators of the Askey-Wilson algebra. This relationship allows us to leverage the representation of the algebra to compute the exact partition function for the theory on the three-sphere, where the deformation is fixed. This approach also enables us to recover the level-asymptotic limit, which matches the calculation from Chern-Simons theory on the three-sphere using classical fields. Furthermore, we can establish a precise finite-level decomposition of the three-sphere partition function in terms of the asymptotic values of the Wilson loops. This method can be extended to calculate partition functions for general graphs in the theory with gauge group $SU(2)$.

The geometric structure of low-dimensional fermion systems is heavily influenced by the lattice choice made to model the system's geometry. In this research, a novel approach utilizes the triangular lattice structure for low-dimensional systems, which is implemented via a time-dependent variational Monte Carlo technique. By transitioning from a standard single-site basis to one centered on trimers, we demonstrate that this change significantly reduces the quantum Monte Carlo sign problem at low temperatures. To validate our method, we provide mathematical derivations and numerical simulations for the spinless fermi gas and fermionic superfluid models in one and two-dimensional systems.

The effectiveness of large language models in few-shot and zero-shot learning tasks is well established, with their higher architectures achieving better results on tasks like image classification and visual question answering. Nonetheless, the direct impact of model size on their generalization capabilities is still unclear. To investigate this phenomenon, we examine the relationship between the size of pre-trained language models and their performance on image classification tasks. Our findings reveal a strong correlation between the number of parameters and achievable AUC-ROC scores across the datasets we evaluated, with larger models consistently achieving higher scores. We also discovered that, on most datasets, the difference in performance between the largest and smallest models is substantial, with few exceptions. Moreover, we observed that smaller models tend to benefit more from pre-training on larger scales than larger models, with some small models showing significant improvements when trained on a larger scale.

In this study, we revisit the relationship between Higgs inflation and the MSSM in its various forms, specifically focusing on a two-Higgs doublet model with an extended supersymmetric framework. We have made two key findings: (i) LHC analyses have significantly reduced the available parameter space for next-to-minimal supersymmetric scenarios, with predictions of a strong first-order phase transition now requiring fine-tuning. (ii) In an effort to resolve the super-CMW problem, adding a gauge singlino to the MSSM particle spectrum has the potential to address the mu problem, while also addressing the constraints imposed by the Higgs data.

The upcoming experiment ALPICA, a compact interferometer operating at millimeter wavelengths, is set to launch in Japan and will be designed to detect robust redshifts in the  z=2-4 range of the ERS. Atacama Large Millimeter Array (ALMA) is currently capable of detecting about 10% of the ERS at those redshifts, but it's limited by its short observing sessions of five hours. On the other hand, the ALPICA is specifically designed for deep  z spectroscopy and is intended to be used for a variety of applications at millimeter wavelengths, including those for the detection of star-forming galaxies at the epoch of reionization. With its high spectral resolution of 300 and a versatile array configuration, ALPICA can be set up in various setups to provide various beam sizes, ranging from 1.5 to 15 arcseconds. This allows for the detection of galaxies at the epoch of reionization with a high degree of spatial resolution.

A low-energy electromagnetic excitation spectrum derived from a many-body wave function overlap method reveals the behavior of Dirac semimetal systems near a magnetic quantum critical point in a well-established two-dimensional ferromagnet, namely the two-dimensional Heisenberg model. Specifically, the computed over-lap method results show that the proximity to a Dirac spin liquid ground state, the theoretically proposed MBLICQ state, is associated with the emergence of two in-plane monopole excitations with a low-energy dipole transition. Notably, the computed energy of these in-plane monopole excitations, derived from a finite-size scaling of the many-body overlap method, is significantly lower than that resulting from spin-wave theory. As the magnetic field increases towards the MBLICQ state, the in-plane excitations of the monopoles become the lowest lying excitations in the system, in stark contrast to the predictions of spin-wave theory. Moreover, the finite many-body overlap method results also reveal a substantial enhancement in the transition strength of the low-energy monopole excitations, the so-called low-k monopole transition form factor, which can be directly observed in experimental measurements such as inelastic neutron scattering in a three-dimensional spin-1/2 system, such as the recently discovered spinice. Consequently, the finite many-body overlap method results suggest a feasible experimental detection of low-lying in-plane monopole excitations in a three-dimensional spin-1/2 system, the so-called three-dimensional spinice.

The breaking of symmetries in lattice systems is analyzed with a focus on systems that break the $Z_3$ symmetry explicitly. This is done by deviating from the conditions that maximize the range of the cat state in a system with a $Z_3$ symmetry, specifically in a system that is a time and space symmetric Ising model on a Euclidean lattice. It is found that this deviation, or perturbation, is not a small effect but rather a significant one when expressed in terms of the optimal $Z_3$ breaking parameter. However, this perturbation can be made smaller by increasing the number of sites in the time direction. Specifically, this results in a weaker violation of the $Z_3$ symmetry, as shown by the effective $Z_3$-odd cat potential scaling as $1/N_t$ for small values of this potential. This effect can be further supported by the observed rapid thermalization of cat states, even with a low transverse field, when a $Z_3$ symmetry is violated.

A new model for calculating the rarefaction of gases has been developed, which takes into consideration the non-equilibrium distribution of gases as an sum of localized distributions. This model, known as the $\upsilon$-model, was tested using the Boltzmann equation and was found to accurately predict thermal transpiration in certain micro-flows, outperforming other models in this scenario.

This study introduces a novel approach to few-shot semantic parsing that leverages abundant unlabeled data, substantially enhancing performance. A unified framework encompasses data extraction, parsing, and alignment under a single abstract representation. A neural extractor transforms specific linguistic features into parameters of this representation. A learned alignment model adjusts these parameters to optimize parsing accuracy on a few labeled instances. A neural parser consumption model parses the aligned abstract representation to generate semantic interpretations. Additionally, this study defines aligned sequence labels to reduce annotation effort. Experiments on the RESTL-22 dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, significantly increasing parsing accuracy over state-of-the-art models and facilitating a 10x reduction in data requirements.

The experiments at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) that operate within the proton-proton environment have reached a saturation point with current Monolithic Active Pixel Sensor (MLAPS) and Low Gain Avalanche Diode (LGAD) technologies due to the increasing luminosity of the upgraded LHC (LHC Run 3) and the upcoming High-Luminosity LHC (HL-LHC). To bridge this gap, novel approaches to these technologies are being explored, including optimized fabrication processes, innovative designs, and alternative technologies. One promising direction involves transitioning from indium tin oxide (ISO) to copper as a conductive material for front-illuminated sensors. This study delves into novel manufacturing methods for front-illuminated AC-coupled Low Gain Pre-amplifiers using copper, developing optimized processes that leverage copper's superior properties compared to ISO. Results from non-functionalized copper AC-coupled Low Gain Pre-amplifiers are presented, showcasing improved performance and reduced cost compared to their ISO counterparts. These advancements hold promise for future MLAPS developments.
